title: Set up the model
task: Write the two resource rows yourself before copying. Which row contains the coefficient 2?
code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog
np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True)
A = np.array([[1., 1.], [2., 1.]])
c = np.array([3., 2.])  # Contributions, not minimization coefficients.
b = np.array([4., 5.])
def solve(c=(3., 2.), b=(4., 5.), matrix=A, bounds=(0, None)):
    result = linprog(-np.asarray(c, dtype=float),
                     A_ub=matrix, b_ub=np.asarray(b, dtype=float),
                     bounds=bounds, method="highs")
    if not result.success:
        raise RuntimeError(result.message)
    return result
print("Resource matrix:", A, sep="\n")
print("Contributions:", c)
print("Capacities:", b)
script: Open a Python editor with NumPy and SciPy available. Follow the setup instructions on this page if the imports fail. Run the blocks in order, in the same session. In the first block, enter the resource matrix with one row per constraint and one column per product. The second row is two, one. Keep positive contribution coefficients here; our helper function changes their signs when calling the minimization solver. Predict the matrix and vectors that will print, run the block, and compare. Nothing is optimized yet. This step checks that the computer model matches the problem you intended to write.

title: Solve and read the baseline
task: Predict production, contribution and unused capacity. Run, then compare all three.
code:
base = solve()
print("success:", base.success)
print("production:", base.x)
print("minimized objective:", base.fun)
print("max contribution:", -base.fun)
print("resource slack:", base.ineqlin.residual)
print("row marginals:", base.ineqlin.marginals)
assert np.allclose(base.x, [1, 3])
assert np.isclose(-base.fun, 9)
script: Run the baseline solver block. First check success. If it is false, stop and diagnose the model instead of interpreting a solution vector. With the supplied data, production should be one and three. The minimized objective is negative nine, while maximum contribution is positive nine. Both resource slacks should be zero. Notice the negative row marginals. Don't relabel them as negative resource values. They refer to the minimized negative contribution. Pause and explain each printed line in your own words before opening the expected output.

production: [1. 3.]
minimized objective: -9.0
max contribution: 9.0
resource slack: [0. 0.]
row marginals: [-1. -1.]

title: Verify the plan without trusting the solver
task: Check the infeasible candidate (2,2). Explain why contribution 10 cannot beat the optimum.
code:
x = base.x
use = A @ x
slack = b - use
print("resource use:", use)
print("computed slack:", slack)
print("computed contribution:", c @ x)
assert np.all(x >= -1e-9)
assert np.all(slack >= -1e-9)
bad = np.array([2., 2.])
print("candidate (2,2) resource use:", A @ bad)
print("candidate feasible:", bool(np.all(A @ bad <= b)))
vertices = np.array([[0,0], [2.5,0], [1,3], [0,4]])
print("vertex contributions:", vertices @ c)
script: Now verify the returned plan independently. Multiply the original resource matrix by production and subtract from capacities. This should reproduce the reported slacks. Also compute contribution directly from the positive coefficients. Then test the tempting candidate two, two. Its contribution is ten, but resource two would require six units. The candidate is infeasible and must be rejected. Finally, compare the four vertex contributions. This gives a small geometric check independent of the solver's status. Use tolerances for floating-point calculations rather than expecting every computed zero to be printed identically.

title: Solve the dual explicitly
task: Why do we negate both A transpose and c in the dual inequalities?
code:
dual = linprog(b, A_ub=-A.T, b_ub=-c,
               bounds=(0, None), method="highs")
assert dual.success, dual.message
prices = dual.x
print("dual prices:", prices)
print("dual slack:", A.T @ prices - c)
print("dual objective:", dual.fun)
print("duality gap:", dual.fun + base.fun)
assert np.all(A.T @ prices >= c - 1e-9)
assert np.isclose(dual.fun, -base.fun)
script: Write the dual on paper first: minimize four u plus five v, with covering inequalities greater than or equal to the contribution coefficients. SciPy accepts the inequality rows in less-than-or-equal form. Therefore negate both sides of those covering inequalities: use negative A transpose and negative c. The dual objective stays positive b. Run the block. You should obtain resource prices one and one and dual objective nine. Verify the dual slacks and the gap. Equal feasible objective values certify optimality. Negating only one side of an inequality would create the wrong model.
output:
dual prices: [1. 1.]
dual slack: [0. 0.]
dual objective: 9.0
duality gap: 0.0

title: Check complementarity and signs
task: Explain why a zero product does not prove feasibility by itself.
code:
resource_slack = b - A @ base.x
dual_slack = A.T @ prices - c
products = np.r_[prices * resource_slack, base.x * dual_slack]
print("complementarity products:", products)
print("profit shadow prices:", -base.ineqlin.marginals)
print("max reduced costs:", c - A.T @ prices)
assert np.allclose(products, 0)
assert np.allclose(prices, -base.ineqlin.marginals)
assert np.allclose(c - A.T @ prices, -base.lower.marginals)
script: Compute each complementary product separately. The first pair multiplies resource price by unused capacity. The second pair multiplies production by its dual slack. All four should vanish for this feasible primal and dual pair. Also compare the explicit dual prices with the negatives of the solver's row marginals. They agree for this formulation. The final line checks the relationship to lower-bound marginals in this example with nonnegative variables and no finite upper bounds. Don't generalize that sign test to variables at upper bounds without examining the formulation.
output:
complementarity products: [0. 0. 0. 0.]
profit shadow prices: [1. 1.]
max reduced costs: [0. 0.]

title: Perturb one capacity at a time
task: Predict both production vectors before running. Why must each trial start from the original b?
code:
h = 0.1
for i in range(2):
    changed = b.copy()  # Reset for each independent trial.
    changed[i] += h
    trial = solve(b=changed)
    min_slope = (trial.fun - base.fun) / h
    profit_slope = (-trial.fun + base.fun) / h
    print("resource", i+1, "production", trial.x,
          "min slope", round(min_slope, 6),
          "profit slope", round(profit_slope, 6))
    assert np.isclose(profit_slope, prices[i])
script: Before running, predict what happens when resource one increases by one tenth. Then predict an independent increase of resource two. Each trial must start from a fresh copy of the original capacities. Otherwise the second experiment measures a simultaneous change instead. The production vectors should be zero point nine, three point two, and one point one, two point nine. Both contribution gains are one tenth. The minimized-objective slope is negative one; the contribution slope is positive one. This numerical experiment makes the marginal-sign conversion visible, rather than relying on memorization.
output:
resource 1 production [0.9 3.2] min slope -1.0 profit slope 1.0
resource 2 production [1.1 2.9] min slope -1.0 profit slope 1.0

title: Discover the range for resource one
task: At b1=6, calculate the old prediction before reading the actual result. Explain the discrepancy.
code:
for b1 in [2, 2.5, 4, 4.5, 5, 6]:
    r = solve(b=(b1, 5))
    old_plan = np.array([5-b1, 2*b1-5])
    old_prediction = 9 + (b1-4)
    print("b1", b1, "plan", r.x, "value", round(-r.fun, 4),
          "old plan feasible", bool(np.all(old_plan >= 0)),
          "old predicted value", old_prediction)
    expected = min(3*b1, b1+5, 10)
    assert np.isclose(-r.fun, expected)
print("At 2.5 and 5, left and right slopes differ.")

title: Resource two and simultaneous changes
task: Explain why the separate allowable ranges do not justify capacities (5,4).
code:
for b2 in [3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9]:
    r = solve(b=(4, b2))
    expected = min(2*b2, b2+4, 12)
    assert np.isclose(-r.fun, expected)
    print("b2", b2, "plan", r.x, "value", round(-r.fun, 4))
b1, b2 = 5., 4.
joint_plan = np.array([b2-b1, 2*b1-b2])
joint = solve(b=(b1,b2))
print("old joint plan:", joint_plan)
print("joint range satisfied:", b1 <= b2 <= 2*b1)
print("actual joint solution:", joint.x, "value", -joint.fun)
assert np.allclose(joint.x, [0,4])

title: Rotate the objective
task: At c1=2 and c1=4, verify an entire edge instead of asserting one solver vector.

for c1 in [1, 2, 3, 3.5, 4, 5]:
    r = solve(c=(c1,2))
    expected = 8 if c1 < 2 else c1+6 if c1 <= 4 else 2.5*c1
    assert np.isclose(-r.fun, expected)
    print("c1", c1, "plan", r.x, "value", round(-r.fun,4))
for point in [[0,4], [0.5,3.5], [1,3]]:

    assert np.isclose(np.dot([4,2], point), 10)

title: Introduce a new product and reoptimize
task: Compute its old reduced cost. How far can x=1-t, y=3 continue?
code:
A3 = np.column_stack([A, [1.,2.]])
for ct in [2,3,4]:
    c3 = np.array([3.,2.,ct])
    r = solve(c=c3, matrix=A3)
    print("ct", ct, "old reduced cost", ct-3,
          "plan", r.x, "value", round(-r.fun,4))
    assert np.isclose(-r.fun, 10 if ct==4 else 9)
new_prices = np.array([0.,2.])
new_c = np.array([3.,2.,4.])
assert np.all(A3.T @ new_prices >= new_c - 1e-9)
for point in [[0,3,1], [0,2,1.5], [0,0,2.5]]:
    assert np.all(A3 @ point <= b + 1e-9)
    assert np.isclose(new_c @ point, b @ new_prices)
print("Alternative new-product optima certified at value 10.")
script: Add a third column to the resource matrix, not a third constraint row. The new column is one, two. At the old prices its resource value is three. Test contributions two, three, and four. The corresponding reduced costs are negative one, zero, and positive one. With contribution four, the old exchange replaces x by t only until t reaches one. title: Interpret a lower-bound marginal
task: Predict the loss from forcing x>=0.1 under objective x+3y.
code:
changed_objective = solve(c=(1,3))
forced = solve(c=(1,3), bounds=[(0.1,None),(0,None)])
print("baseline plan:", changed_objective.x)
print("row marginals:", changed_objective.ineqlin.marginals)
print("lower-bound marginals:", changed_objective.lower.marginals)
print("forced plan:", forced.x)
print("profit loss:", round(-changed_objective.fun + forced.fun, 6))
assert np.allclose(forced.x, [0.1,3.9])
assert np.isclose(-changed_objective.fun + forced.fun, 0.2)

Inspect the lower-bound marginal of x, which should be positive two for the minimized objective. Now impose a lower bound of zero point one on x. The new plan is zero point one, three point nine, and contribution falls by zero point two. Multiply by one hundred to obtain a twenty-dollar daily loss. This sensitivity belongs to a variable bound. title: Choose capacity by net benefit
task: Choose among A, B, C and no purchase before revealing the outputs.
code:
baseline_dollars = -solve().fun * 100
offers = [("None",0,0), ("A",0.5,30), ("B",1,70), ("C",2,90)]
results = []
for name,q,cost in offers:
    gross = -solve(b=(4+q,5)).fun*100 - baseline_dollars
    net = gross - cost
    results.append((net,name))
    print(name, "gross gain", round(gross,2),
          "cost", cost, "net benefit", round(net,2))
best = max(results)
print("best package:", best[1], "net benefit:", round(best[0],2))
assert best[1] == "B"
qs = np.linspace(0,2,201)
nets = np.array([-solve(b=(4+q,5)).fun*100-baseline_dollars-60*q for q in qs])
q_best = qs[np.argmax(nets)]
print("divisible capacity: q =", q_best, "net =", round(max(nets),2))
assert np.isclose(q_best,1)
script: Evaluate each complete offer by reoptimizing, then subtract its purchase cost exactly once. Include the no-purchase option. Offer A adds half a unit, B adds one, and C adds two. The largest package is not the best: its extra resource cannot all be used productively. The expected net benefits are twenty, thirty, and ten dollars per day, so B wins. The final calculation changes the pricing assumption to divisible capacity at sixty dollars per unit. It finds one unit as the best purchase. Explain why these are two different decision problems.

title: Diagnose failures and attempt the exercises

code:
infeasible = linprog([1.], A_ub=[[1.],[-1.]], b_ub=[1.,-2.],
                     bounds=(None,None), method="highs")
unbounded = linprog([-1.], bounds=(0,None), method="highs")
print("infeasible success/status:", infeasible.success, infeasible.status)
print("unbounded success/status:", unbounded.success, unbounded.status)
assert not infeasible.success and infeasible.status == 2
assert not unbounded.success and unbounded.status == 3
print("Do not interpret failed solves as optimal production plans.")
